title: What can a bitcoin: link ask a wallet to do?
dek: A bitcoin: link carries an address, an amount and other ways to pay, all in one link. BIP 321 says which parts a wallet must understand and which it may ignore.

blocks.text: Click a payment link on a web page, or scan a QR code, and a wallet opens with the payment filled in. Both carry the same thing: a `bitcoin:` URI. It is a request, not a payment: a wallet MUST NOT act on it without the user's approval.

BIP 21, from 2012, set out the scheme. BIP 321 replaces it and describes how links were used by 2024: several ways to pay in one link, keys in any letter case, and room for new payment methods that older wallets can safely skip.

figure.title: One link, read by three wallets
figure.caption: Choose one of BIP 321's example links. The model cuts it into parts, decodes the values, and reads it as three illustrative wallets would, each implementing different keys. The example addresses are intentionally invalid.

blocks.text: A link is `bitcoin:`, an address, and optional parameters after a question mark, joined by ampersands. The address MUST be a base58 P2SH or P2PKH address, a bech32 SegWit version 0 or bech32m SegWit address, or empty.

`amount` is in decimal BTC, with a period and no commas: `amount=50.00` and `amount=50` both mean 50 BTC. `label` names the recipient and `message` describes the payment. Characters outside the allowed set are encoded as UTF-8 and then percent-encoded, so a space becomes `%20`.

blocks.title: A payment link, part by part
blocks.caption: BIP 321's 50 BTC example, one part to a row. The model percent-decodes its message.

blocks.text: The scheme and the parameter keys are case-insensitive, while values and addresses can be case-sensitive. BIP 21 had made the keys case-sensitive, but QR codes mostly use uppercase, so reading keys in any case was already common.

blocks.title: Lowercase and uppercase
blocks.caption: The same two SegWit addresses as a lowercase and an uppercase link, both from BIP 321's examples. Keys are case-insensitive, and BIP 321 says all-uppercase links should be handled fine; read in either case, both give the same payment instructions.

sections.heading: More than one way to pay

blocks.text: Parameters can carry other ways to pay: `lightning` for a BOLT 11 invoice, `lno` for a BOLT 12 offer, `pay` for BIP 351 and `sp` for a Silent Payments address. These keys may repeat. New bech32 and bech32m formats SHOULD use their human-readable part as the key, which is why two SegWit addresses can appear as two `bc` parameters.

The address may be left out when at least one instruction is given, for a recipient who wants no on-chain fallback. Future address formats SHOULD go into parameters rather than the address, so that a wallet that only understands the address can still pay.

One rule makes this safe. A wallet can safely ignore any parameter it does not implement, unless the key starts with `req-`: if it does not implement a required key, it MUST consider the whole link invalid. The hero's first wallet shows both sides. It pays a Lightning link's on-chain fallback, and it refuses a link with a `req-` key it does not know.
Some keys must not repeat. Two labels, two messages or two `pop` values make a link invalid, and BIP 321's invalid examples add two amounts.

A link MAY include `pop`, a percent-encoded URI prefix. After paying, a wallet that supports it SHOULD decode the prefix once, append the key it paid with (`onchain` for the address), an equals sign and the payment information, and open the result. The payment information is the full transaction, witness data included, in hex, or, for a BOLT 11 invoice, the hex-encoded payment preimage.

blocks.title: Proof of payment
blocks.caption: Four of BIP 321's five proof-of-payment examples. The model builds the two published callbacks shown here (its tests build all four the BIP publishes), and follows the rules for the two that point at a web page.

blocks.text: A wallet MUST NOT open a callback that would open a web browser, such as an `https` one. The author's reason is privacy: proof URIs must only be opened when they will simply switch back to the local app that started the payment, without revealing the sender's IP address to the recipient. If the parameter was `req-pop` and the wallet will not open it, because the scheme is unsafe or it cannot return payment information for the method it used, the wallet MUST NOT pay at all.

Best practice is a fresh address for every on-chain payment, so a link with an on-chain address MUST NOT stand for personal details, but for a one-time payment instruction. A link that carries only reusable instructions, such as a BOLT 12 offer or a Silent Payments address, MAY be reused.

blocks.label: Caveat
blocks.text: The example links use deliberately invalid addresses, as BIP 321 notes, and placeholder invoices. Never treat them as payment requests.

BIP 21 allowed only base58 addresses, and its text made parameter keys case-sensitive. Compared with it, BIP 321 adds standard keys for other payment instructions, makes keys case-insensitive, allows bech32 and bech32m addresses and an empty address, and adds proof of payment.
BIP 21 (Nils Schneider and Matt Corallo) was assigned in 2012 and is recorded as Closed. BIP 321 (Matt Corallo) was assigned in 2024 and is recorded as Complete.
